The output of the self-attention mechanism (i.e., the weighted values) is typically used as
intermediate representations in sequence processing tasks, and these representations are further
processed by subsequent network layers to predict the next word or perform other tasks. Thus,
the self-attention mechanism provides a flexible internal representation, offering each element in
the sequence a contextual representation that synthesizes information from the entire sequence.
The design of the Transformer model nests multiple identical processing layers. Through multi-
level data processing, the self-attention mechanism can capture representations at different
levels, for example, from individual words or characters to more complex semantic concepts
and relationships. Each layer is able to learn more abstract representations of information
from the previous layer’s output. This hierarchical processing helps the model understand the
complex structure of language, including syntactic and semantic information. With multilevel
data processing, the model not only distills information but also integrates and re-encodes
it to generate richer and more complex representations. This process involves capturing and
integrating information from different parts of the sequence to support complex reasoning and
comprehension tasks.
The discussion so far has explained how Transformer self-attention uses learned transformations,
similarity scores, normalization, masking, and weighted sums to build contextual token
representations. The next section extends this idea by showing how the Transformer uses multiple
attention heads in parallel, allowing the model to capture different types of relationships within
the same sequence.
Exploring the design of multi-head attention
In the Transformer model, the multi-head attention mechanism is implemented by combining
multiple attention mechanisms. Each attention mechanism is called a head, and multiple heads
work in parallel, with each head learning different representations. This mechanism enables the
model to focus on different parts of the sequence simultaneously when processing sequences. For
example, some heads may focus on the syntactic structure of the sentence, others may focus on
the semantic information, while others might focus on sentiment information. Through the
multi-head attention mechanism, the model can model sequences from different perspectives,
thereby enhancing its expressive and generalization capabilities.

For these workflow-like workloads, Azure Durable Functions and Logic Apps are the main ser -
vices you would use. Logic Apps ships with hundreds of pre-built connectors and allows you to
create workflows in minutes. Durable Functions requires development skills as it makes use of the
Durable Framework, which you can integrate into your application. It is worth mentioning that

with well-known third-party services (SaaS platforms) or integrate different systems. You could
use Durable Functions whenever you need orchestrations that are scoped to a single application.
Hybrid services, our last top-level group, rely on on-premises agents that initiate outbound con -
nections to Azure, creating a bi-directional communication channel for exchanging data. This
approach is especially useful when there’s no private peering between Azure data centers and
on-premises environments, or when a cloud-based service needs to interact with on-premises
systems. By running the agent locally, hybrid services can support protocols such as NTLM and
Kerberos—common in on-premises setups but not natively supported by most PaaS offerings.
For example, Azure Hybrid Connections allow Azure App Service to consume an on-premises
database seamlessly, without the need to expose the on-premises database to the internet or to
have private connectivity between the two worlds.

Passkey (FIDO2) authentication
Passkeys, developed idx_37d436c5 by the FIDO (Fast Identity Online) Alliance, offer an innovative approach
to secure authentication. They eliminate the need for traditional idx_1481e68c passwords by leveraging
FIDO2 standards. These keys depend on public key cryptography to authenticate identities,
offering a idx_86d97b41 higher level of security by minimizing vulnerabilities such as phishing, password-
related breaches, and weak passwords. By replacing passwords with cryptographic credentials,
passkeys simplify the sign-in process while enhancing protection against cyber threats.
Passkeys are supported on modern systems like Windows 10 (version 1903 or higher) and are
integrated into tools like the Microsoft Authenticator, empowering organizations to adopt
robust, password-free security solutions.
As per idx_857953d7 the FIDO2 specification, each security key vendor must provide an Authenticator
Attestation GUID (AAGUID). The AAGUID is a 128-bit identifier that specifies the key type.
Passkey providers on desktops and mobiles are also expected to provide an AAGUID during
registration. Before enabling passkeys, ensure that the following requirements have been met:
Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication should be enabled in the organization.

In observability, if you asked " How is the system health today? ", an assistant with RAG
capabilities would check real-time metrics and logs before answering. The answer wouldn't be
immediate but would be highly accurate.
CAG offers an alternative: load a bunch of context and then respond. If the same person wakes
up and gathers information about the current state of the world, they can then answer
questions without external lookups. This allows them to also respond more quickly when
asked questions. In the case of computing, CAG is great for tightly scoped datasets with
infrequent updates, such as runbooks.
Using the same example, you would also include a log file: " Review these logs and tell me, how is
the system health today? " The answer you'd get would be nearly immediate, and it would also be
correct based on the logs. But if, in the minute between log retrieval and starting the session
with the AI assistant, the system crashed, the answer could be out of date.
However, if you had an AI agent troubleshooting idx_19888376 an alert, and the alert information along with
a runbook was supplied upfront, then the agent would be able to return the results of that
runbook execution very idx_abed508a quickly because the process of using that additional context was
already there.
There are pros and cons to both approaches. CAG has limits on how much data can be
referenced since it must all be placed in a cache upfront, but that data is available more quickly,
so any prompts that rely on the cached data will return results faster than they would with
RAG.
RAG is less limiting because, while the process of doing the lookup adds additional time to the
response, the data can be in real time, which would be useful for understanding software
health or the current state of an application by parsing the observability metrics.
While RAG and CAG systems can stand on their own, that would be a very atypical use case for
them, as they're often used as an augmentation to an LLM, bringing in newer or external data
to the model beyond its training data. RAG and CAG are both also different from fine-tuning,
which is a specific method of adding new data to an LLM's training data. Unlike RAG and CAG,
where the augmenting data remains distinct, fine-tuning allows users of AI systems to extend
the system's knowledge into a specific domain of expertise, especially against data that is
proprietary.
For all three types of generation (LLM, RAG, and CAG), the data relied upon can be indexed and
weighted to help the AI system provide a more accurate response. This is an important aspect
of ensuring quality in an AIOps system, as it's a protective measure against errors and failures.
